AURORA BOREALIS

Nature's most dramatic light show — caused by charged particles from the Sun colliding with Earth's magnetic field. Green curtains at 110 km, crimson arches at 300 km, violet fringes from nitrogen — all dancing above the Arctic in silence.

HOW THE AURORA FORMS

01
☀️

Solar Wind & CMEs

The Sun emits a continuous stream of electrons and protons called the solar wind. During solar flares and coronal mass ejections (CMEs), billions of tons of magnetized plasma are hurled toward Earth at 1–3 million km/h — arriving in 1–4 days.

→
02
🧲

Magnetic Reconnection

Earth's magnetosphere deflects most solar wind. But when the interplanetary magnetic field (IMF) Bz component turns southward, it connects with Earth's northward field — a process called magnetic reconnection — opening a channel for particles to flow inward.

→
03
⚡

Particle Acceleration

Charged particles accelerate along magnetic field lines toward the polar regions, guided by Earth's dipole field. This is why aurora concentrates in oval-shaped rings around the geomagnetic poles, typically between 65°–72°N latitude.

→
04
💡

Atmospheric Excitation

Particles collide with oxygen and nitrogen atoms at 80–300 km altitude. These atoms absorb the energy and re-emit it as visible light. The altitude and gas type determine the color — green from oxygen at 110 km, red above 200 km, blue-violet from nitrogen molecules.

WHAT CAUSES EACH COLOR

Green

Oxygen · 100–150 km altitude

The most common aurora color. Atomic oxygen at ~110 km emits the characteristic 557.7 nm green line. Almost every aurora display shows green — it's the dominant color in the auroral oval.

Red

Oxygen · 200–300 km altitude

Rare red aurora appears at high altitude where the atmosphere is thinner. The same oxygen atom at 630 nm emits red — but only when collision frequency is low enough not to quench the emission. Visible during strong storms (Kp 7+).

Blue / Violet

Nitrogen molecules · 80–100 km

Ionized nitrogen molecules (N₂⁺) produce blue and violet light at lower altitudes. Often visible at the lower edge of green curtains as a blue fringe. Also creates the purple in mixed displays.

Pink / Magenta

Nitrogen + Oxygen mix · 90–100 km

Pink aurora appears when nitrogen emissions at the lower edge of a green aurora layer blend together. Often forms the lowest, brightest portions of active aurora curtains during substorm events.

White / Yellow

Mixed green + red + blue

When aurora is very bright and intense, the eye's color receptors saturate and the mixed light appears white or yellowish. Also common in fast-moving, structureless "veil" aurora during substorm onset.

STEVE (Mauve)

Sub-Auroral Ion Drift · 100–130 km

Strong Thermal Emission Velocity Enhancement — a narrow, mauve-colored arc running east-west, distinct from traditional aurora. Discovered by citizen scientists in 2016. Caused by a hot, fast plasma stream, not by particle precipitation.

READING SPACE WEATHER DATA

The Kp Index

The Planetary K-index (Kp) is the primary metric for geomagnetic activity, measured globally on a scale of 0–9. Updated every 3 hours by NOAA.

Kp 0 No aurora
Kp 1 Polar regions only
Kp 2 70°N+
Kp 3 65°N+ — Iceland, Norway
Kp 4 60°N+ — Scotland, Canada
Kp 5 55°N+ — Northern US
Kp 6 50°N+ — N. Germany
Kp 7 45°N+ — Central Europe
Kp 8 40°N+ — Southern Europe
Kp 9 35°N+ — Major storm

Kp 5+ triggers the G-scale (G1–G5). The May 2024 storm reached Kp 9 — aurora was visible as far south as Florida and Texas.

The Bz Component

Bz is the north-south component of the interplanetary magnetic field (IMF). It's the single most important real-time indicator for aurora.

▼
Southward Bz (negative)

When Bz points south (negative values), the IMF connects with Earth's field via magnetic reconnection. Solar particles stream into the magnetosphere. Aurora intensifies. The more negative Bz is, the better — values of −20 nT or below indicate major storm conditions.

▲
Northward Bz (positive)

When Bz points north (positive values), Earth's magnetosphere is shielded. Solar particles are deflected away. Aurora is suppressed even during otherwise active conditions. A storm can "turn off" instantly when Bz flips northward.

PRO TIP

Watch for Bz to go strongly negative (−10 nT or lower) and stay that way for 20+ minutes. That sustained southward field drives the best aurora displays. Short dips often don't sustain long enough to cause major activity.

Solar Wind Speed

Solar wind speed affects how fast magnetic disturbances travel. Faster wind = stronger dynamic pressure on the magnetosphere.

250–350 km/sSlow — weak activity even with southward Bz
350–500 km/sAverage — typical aurora conditions
500–700 km/sFast — enhanced aurora even with moderate Bz
700+ km/sStorm-level — associated with CME arrival

BEST PLACES TO SEE THE AURORA

🇳🇴

Tromsø, Norway

69.6°N

The world's undisputed aurora capital, sitting directly under the auroral oval. Dark polar nights from November to February. Excellent infrastructure — guided tours, snowmobile safaris, glass-roofed cabins. Minimum Kp needed: 2.

BEST OVERALL Oct – Mar
🇮🇸

Iceland

64–66°N

Vast dark landscapes, geothermal hot springs under the stars, black sand beaches lit by dancing light. Kp 3 is usually enough. The South Coast and Snæfellsnes Peninsula offer particularly dark skies. Minimum Kp: 3.

HIGHLY RECOMMENDED Sep – Apr
🇫🇮

Finnish Lapland

68–70°N

Saariselkä and Luosto average 200+ aurora nights per year. Magical winter scenery — snow-laden forests, frozen lakes, reindeer. Glass-roofed aurora cabins let you watch from bed. Minimum Kp: 2.

GLASS CABINS Nov – Mar
🇺🇸

Fairbanks, Alaska

64.8°N

Inside the auroral zone with extremely clear, cold, dry nights. Poker Flat Research Range is the world's largest land-based rocket range for aurora research. UAF Geophysical Institute provides excellent local forecasts. Minimum Kp: 2.

RESEARCH HUB Oct – Mar
🇨🇦

Yukon, Canada

60–65°N

Whitehorse sits directly under the auroral oval. Extraordinarily clear skies, very low humidity, and minimal light pollution. The Aurora Viewing Village at Takhini Hot Springs is a popular winter destination. Minimum Kp: 2.

HIGHLY RECOMMENDED Aug – Apr
🇳🇿

Otago, New Zealand

44–46°S

Southern Aurora (Aurora Australis) is visible from the South Island during moderate to strong storms. Lake Tekapo and the Mackenzie Basin have internationally-protected dark skies. Minimum Kp for visibility: 5.

AURORA AUSTRALIS Mar – Sep

WHEN TO GO

🍂

Autumn (Sep – Nov)

Equinox seasons (around Sep 22 and Mar 20) see enhanced geomagnetic activity — Earth's magnetic field is more vulnerable at the equinoxes. September and October combine long dark nights with statistically elevated Kp. Best value aurora travel window.

❄️

Winter (Dec – Feb)

Maximum darkness — polar nights above 67°N mean up to 24 hours of darkness per day. Cold air is dry and clear. Fewer clouds than autumn. The tradeoff: extremely cold temperatures and shorter windows for comfortable outdoor viewing.

🌸

Spring (Mar – Apr)

Second equinox peak — March equinox brings statistically the highest average Kp of the year. Longer nights than autumn in the northern hemisphere but still dark enough. Temperatures are milder. April often sees strong G2–G3 storms.

☀️

Summer (Jun – Aug)

Midnight sun above the Arctic Circle means the sky never gets truly dark. Aurora still occurs — the magnetosphere is active — but it's invisible in the bright sky. The exception: powerful G4–G5 storms can produce aurora visible even in twilight.

🌙 Moon Phase Matters

🌑 New Moon

Maximum darkness. Best conditions for faint aurora, long-exposure photography, and seeing the Milky Way alongside the aurora.

🌓 Quarter Moon

Acceptable — sets early or rises late. Plan your viewing window around the moon's position. Check moonrise/moonset times for your location.

🌕 Full Moon

Brightens the sky significantly. Faint aurora (Kp 1–3) may be washed out. Strong displays (Kp 5+) are still visible and can create beautiful moonlit aurora landscapes.

PHOTOGRAPHING THE AURORA

📷 DSLR / Mirrorless Settings

SettingValueNotes
ISO800 – 3200 Start at ISO 1600 and adjust. Avoid noise by not going too high.
Aperturef/1.4 – f/2.8 As wide as your lens allows. f/1.8 is the sweet spot for most lenses.
Shutter5 – 25 sec Use faster shutter (5–8s) for dancing aurora; slower for faint/still aurora.
FocusManual ∞ Autofocus fails at night. Set to infinity, fine-tune on a bright star.
White Balance3500–4200 K Or use RAW and set it in post-processing for maximum flexibility.
FormatRAW (.NEF/.CR3) Never shoot JPEG for aurora. RAW gives 3–4 stops of recovery latitude.
Lens14–24mm Wide-angle captures the full arc. Ultra-wide (14mm) fits more sky.

📱 Smartphone Tips

  • →Use Pro/Manual mode — disable auto-ISO
  • →Set ISO 800–1600, shutter 5–10 seconds
  • →Enable Night Mode on iPhone 14+ / Pixel 6+ — it stacks frames automatically
  • →Use a tripod or rest the phone on something stable — any movement ruins the shot
  • →Use the timer (3s delay) to avoid camera shake when pressing the shutter
  • →Phone cameras often detect aurora before your eyes can see it — take a test shot even for faint displays

🎒 Gear Checklist

  • ✓ Sturdy tripod (carbon fiber for cold)
  • ✓ Wide-angle lens (f/2.8 or faster)
  • ✓ Extra batteries (cold halves capacity)
  • ✓ Intervalometer / remote shutter
  • ✓ Microfibre lens cloth (condensation)
  • ✓ Red-light head torch
  • ✓ Hand warmers (for you and battery)
  • ✓ Battery-powered lens heater
  • ✓ Spare SD cards
  • ✓ NOAA Space Weather app

FREQUENTLY ASKED QUESTIONS

What Kp level do I need to see the aurora?

It depends on your latitude. At 65–70°N (Tromsø, Lapland, Alaska), Kp 2–3 is often enough for a good display. At 55–60°N (Scotland, southern Norway, southern Canada), you need Kp 5+. In central Europe or the northern United States, Kp 7 or higher is typically required. During the historic G5 storm of May 2024, aurora was visible as far south as Florida and the Canary Islands — that required Kp 9.

Why does southward Bz produce aurora?

When the interplanetary magnetic field (IMF) Bz component points south, it aligns anti-parallel with Earth's northward-pointing magnetic field at the dayside magnetopause. This allows magnetic reconnection — where opposing field lines break and reconnect, releasing enormous energy. This opens a portal for solar wind particles to enter the magnetosphere and flow toward the polar regions, driving aurora. The more negative Bz is, the more intense the reconnection and the stronger the aurora.

Why does aurora happen mostly around midnight?

The magnetospheric tail — the night side of Earth's magnetic field, stretched by solar wind pressure — stores energy during the day and releases it explosively in events called substorms, typically peaking around local midnight. Substorm onset triggers rapid brightening of the aurora oval, producing the most dynamic and colourful displays. The hours of 10pm–2am local time consistently produce the best aurora, though displays can occur any time the sky is dark.

Can I see aurora with the naked eye?

Yes — moderate to strong events (Kp 5+) are clearly visible with the naked eye from mid-to-high latitudes as green curtains, arcs, or rays. Weaker displays (Kp 2–4) are often visible to the dark-adapted eye as a faint greenish glow on the horizon, but cameras detect it more easily because camera sensors are more sensitive to the 557.7 nm green wavelength. Always take a test photo before assuming there's nothing to see — you might be surprised.

Are we currently in a good period for aurora?

Yes — Solar Cycle 25 peaked around mid-2025, making 2024–2026 the best aurora-viewing window in over a decade. The May 2024 G5 storm (the strongest since the Halloween Storm of 2003) produced aurora visible worldwide and dramatically demonstrated the power of this solar maximum. Activity typically remains elevated for 1–2 years around the peak before declining toward solar minimum around 2030.

How far in advance can aurora be forecast?

Reliable aurora forecasting is limited to 1–4 days. When a CME is observed leaving the Sun, scientists can predict its Earth-arrival time within ±6 hours. Once the solar wind reaches the DSCOVR satellite at the L1 Lagrange point (1.5 million km from Earth), we have 15–60 minutes of real-time warning before it hits. Kp forecasts for the next 3 hours are highly reliable; 24-hour forecasts are moderately reliable; beyond 3 days is largely speculative. The best strategy: watch NOAA alerts and stay flexible.

What is STEVE and how is it different from aurora?

STEVE (Strong Thermal Emission Velocity Enhancement) appears as a narrow, purple-white or mauve ribbon running east-west across the sky, distinct from the aurora's north-south oriented curtains. It was formally identified and named by citizen scientists in 2016. Unlike aurora — which is caused by energetic particle precipitation — STEVE is caused by a hot, fast-moving stream of ions in the sub-auroral ionosphere at lower latitudes. It often appears alongside traditional aurora but is a separate optical phenomenon.

What is hemispheric power and why does it matter?

Hemispheric Power (HP) is the total power deposited into the polar atmosphere by aurora-causing particles, measured in gigawatts. NOAA estimates it in real-time using satellite data. HP below 30 GW indicates quiet conditions; 30–100 GW is active; above 100 GW indicates strong storm conditions. Unlike Kp (which is updated every 3 hours), HP is derived from real-time measurements and can show rapidly changing aurora intensity within minutes, making it a useful supplementary metric alongside Kp and Bz.
